entries.title: Chicago Archdiocese settles 9 sex abuse claims for $5.4 million
entries.summary: <p>The Archdiocese of Chicago recently settled out of court with nine people who accused eight Chicago-area priests of sexually abusing them decades ago. </p><p>The settlements, totaling $5.4 million, were all reached in the last two weeks, according to the attorneys representing the victims. </p><p>"Nobody's paying that kind of money for something that didn't happen," said Marc Pearlman, one of the victim's attorneys, during a Thursday news conference announcing the settlements. "This is validation that it happened." </p><p>The allegations date as far back as the early 1970s and as recently as the late 1990s. The victims' ages at the time of the abuse ranged from 6 to 14 years old.</p><p>The list of accused priests, most of whom have died, and their Chicago-area parishes are: </p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: In CBP officer's rape trial, woman describes alleged attack at Schaumburg hotel: 'He showed a badge'
entries.summary: <p>A New York woman<b> </b>sobbed<b> </b>at the end of a lengthy day on the witness stand Thursday, after she insisted she’d been “robbed and raped”<b> </b>by a man rumored to be a “fake cop”<b> </b>during a visit to Chicago’s northwest suburbs<b> </b>in 2022.</p><p>She testified during the trial of U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer<b> </b>Luis Uribe, 45. Not only did Uribe work a real job in law enforcement, federal prosecutors say he used his gun and badge to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >sexually assault four women</a><b> </b>in Schaumburg and Naperville.</p><p>But confusion abounded when Uribe’s defense attorney tried to sort through the details of the woman’s visit to the suburb of Schaumburg. The woman is a native of China who became a U.S. citizen in 2003. She speaks little English, so she testified with help from a translator.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" >Border Protection officer accused of sex assaults became ‘perfect mark’ for prostitution ring, lawyer says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>She struggled when it came time to identify Uribe in the courtroom. She told Uribe’s attorney he had things “all messed up”<b> </b>as he tried to identify associates she referred to as “pretty girl,” “beauty”<b> </b>or<b> </b>“sister.”</p><p>However, the woman gave a clear answer when a prosecutor asked what happened to her.</p><p>“He robbed me of my money,” she said. “He raped me.”</p><p>The feds say Uribe committed<b> </b>six attacks<b> </b>between February and October 2022, but his attorney told jurors Wednesday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" target="_blank" >he’d been set up</a> by a prostitution ring overseen by a boss in China. He admitted Uribe visited prostitutes and is a “flawed”<b> </b>human being, but he said there’s no proof that Uribe robbed and raped the women, as prosecutors allege.</p><p>The 67-year-old woman who testified Thursday told jurors she came to Chicago in October 2022 because a friend of hers wanted her “to check out some casinos here.”<b> </b>She said she referred to the friend as “beauty,”<b> </b>and she brought along $3,000.</p><p>She also acknowledged she’d seen a photo of Uribe on the social messaging app WeChat, and she was told he was a “fake cop.”</p><p>The photo was taken during a meeting at a seafood buffet in Hoffman Estates, according to the feds.</p><p>The woman was attacked while staying in a Schaumburg<b> </b>Days Inn, jurors heard. The woman explained Thursday how she heard a knock on her hotel room door and opened it, thinking it was a member of the hotel staff.</p><p>That’s when a man rushed in, she said, wearing a hat, a black jacket and pants.</p><p>“Immediately he closed the door and he showed a badge,”<b> </b>the woman testified.</p><p>He pushed a chair against the door, put the badge and a gun on a table, and asked for cash, she said. The woman told jurors she gave him “all my money.”</p><p>“I was terrified,” she said. “He had a gun.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" >O’Hare-based Border Protection officer sexually abused, robbed women at gunpoint, indictment claims</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>She said he forced her to take off her clothes and perform oral sex. Then, she said, he pulled her to the bed<b> </b>and raped her. When it was over, she said he pushed her into the shower area,<b> </b>put his clothing back on and escaped.</p><p>The woman said she tried to tell the hotel staff she’d been robbed, but she struggled because of her difficulty with English. So she went to a woman she’d met earlier at the hotel — who also happened to be Chinese. </p><p>Early in her testimony, prosecutors asked the alleged victim to identify Uribe in the courtroom. She initially failed to do so and eventually broke down crying, prompting a break in the proceedings. But later, while describing the attack, she pointed and told the translator she’d seen someone who “might be that person.”</p><p>During his cross-examination, defense attorney Michael Clancy<b> </b>asked the woman whether a “boss believed that you were coming to Chicago to work for her and [to] be a sex worker?” The woman said she “didn’t agree”<b> </b>to that arrangement.</p><p>“At my old age, I only agreed to come here to check it out to play,” the woman said, referring to the casinos.</p><p>Still, she admitted learning<b> </b>the second Chinese woman at the hotel was a sex worker.</p><p>Before testimony wrapped for the day, jurors heard the initial testimony of that second woman, who is 54 and also lives in New York. She acknowledged for prosecutors that she did massage work with “a sexual component”<b> </b>and had a “boss”<b> </b>who found her clients.</p><p>She said her boss sent her to the Chicago area<b> </b>in 2022 and showed her the photo of Uribe at the seafood buffet. Then, during her stay at the Schaumburg Days Inn, she said she encountered the first woman “in a terrible state, ready to cry”<b> </b>— and pointing to a photo.</p><p>The woman allegedly told her, “the fake police robbed her and raped her.”</p>

entries.title: Hagen Smith's multi-inning relief assignment could be the recipe for other White Sox starter prospects
entries.summary: <p>Former fifth overall pick <b>Hagen Smith</b> made his first career major league start on Thursday night.</p><p>But his two scoreless innings before giving way to <b>Erick Fedde</b> represents an extension of the White Sox’ league-leading usage of openers, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/24/white-sox-hagen-smith-brian-bannister-will-venable-2024-draft-jac-caglianone-konnor-griffin-trey-yesavage-pitching-development-pete-crow-armstrong" target="_blank" ><u>not a deviation from Smith’s conversion to relief</u></a> for the rest of the season.</p><p>That Smith’s first two full years in pro ball have been defined by a sluggish, physically challenging first halves before a strong finishing kick, is part of why he’s in the bullpen.</p><p>“The last couple of years, the first half of the season has been marred a little bit by an injury -- nothing serious–but in the second half of both last year and what it looks like this year, he’s come back after the injury and been really good,” said Sox farm director <b>Paul Janish</b>.</p><p>With a 0.50 ERA and 26 strikeouts in 18 innings, Smith’s adjustment is going swimmingly, though the 10 walks lend a reliever flavor to his work. With 16 games left, Smith’s role could be the sort of opportunity Triple-A starters <b>Jonathan Cannon, Noah Schultz, Drew Thorpe </b>or <b>David Sandlin </b>should anticipate.</p><p>“It’s very reasonable, as we’ve seen, that they would pitch in a bulk role,” Janish said. “Potentially start as well. But the bulk option is definitely something that they’re aware of and they’re ready for.”</p><p>The most immediate candidate would be Sandlin, who has a 1.90 ERA and 31.7% strikeout rate in four starts since he was last optioned, and is rested after not making his originally scheduled Thursday outing for the Knights.</p><p>“Sandlin’s been locked in,” Janish said. “The integrity of the stuff’s been really good. Feel comfortable saying he’s probably in as confident of a place that he’s been in a little while.”</p><p>Opening day starter <b>Shane Smith </b>is working in single-inning relief in Triple-A for now, but Janish anticipates him competing for a rotation spot next spring.</p><h3><b>Nearly no-hit</b></h3><p>Already limited to five runs in their first two losses to a Pirates team playing out the string, the Sox offense–<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-hitting-director-ryan-fuller-talks-offensive-improvement-and-the-development-that-remains-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u>still their best unit in years</u></a>–did not register a hit off hard-throwing 25-year-old right-hander <b>Jared Jones </b>in Thursday night’s series finale until <b>Colson Montgomery’s </b>two-out double off the wall in seventh.</p><p>In keeping with the theme of the week, the runner was stranded by a <b>Braden Montgomery </b>lineout.</p><h3><b>Antonacci’s identity</b></h3><p><b>Tristan Peters </b>wearing a t-shirt with a picture of <b>Sam Antonacci</b> made to look like a mugshot the day after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-pushing-back-luis-castillo-for-mechanical-work-as-rotation-stays-in-flux-sean-burke-davis-martin-david-sandlin-noah-schultz-drew-thorpe-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>his dustup with Pirates second baseman </u><b><u>Brandon Lowe</u></b></a> might be a coincidence, but is in line with how the team feels about their inflammatory rookie.</p><p>“I don’t think he spends a whole lot of time worrying about making friends,” said Janish. “He has an edge to him. He plays the game hard. I don’t care what era you’re playing in, he was going to be good at this game.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tristan Peters’ disembodied torso is draped in a show of solidarity with Sam Antonacci <a href="https://t.co/ifUteIsQSa">pic.twitter.com/ifUteIsQSa</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2098161260873318484?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Steak and eggs</b></h3><p>Power-hitting prospect <b>Caleb Bonemer </b>will play largely, if not exclusively in the outfield during the Arizona Fall League this October. The position is more demanding on his legs than the infield, but even after 36 home runs, the 20-year-old Bonemer feels fresher than he did at this point last season.</p><p>It’s a credit to his diet and the strength he added in the winter.</p><p>“I was pretty much eating as much steak and eggs as I possibly could,” Bonemer told the Sun-Times.</p>

entries.title: Memories of 9/11 horror still fresh after a quarter-century
entries.summary: <p>On Sept. 11, 2001, my older son was 5, and some mornings played video games on my computer. So I wasn't plugged into the world that morning. I didn't know that American Airlines Flight 11 had struck the North Tower at 7:46 a.m. Chicago time. I did not own a cell phone.</p><p>At the Northbrook Metra station, stepping onto the 8:17 Downtown, I heard a woman down the platform say something about the World Trade Center being hit by a plane.</p><p>At Union Station, knots of people stood around, talking. I asked one: what kind of plane hit the twin towers?</p><p>"A 767," he said. That startled me. I had assumed it would be a Cessna.</p><p>"That's a big plane," I said, thickly.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cd0000" name="module-cd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>At Wacker Drive, people were pouring out of the Sears Tower, fanning out in all directions. I noticed that, as they hurried along, they looked up, scanning the sky. As if they expected to see a plane go into the building at any moment.</p><p>There was a Billy Goat Tavern on Washington, open for breakfast. I stepped inside. Everyone was just standing there in silence, watching the North Tower collapse on TV. I joined them. You could hear the eggs sizzling on the grill.</p><p>The paper was still at 401 N. Wabash. I was on the editorial board and walked into editorial page editor Steve Huntley's office.</p><p>"How do you spell 'Osama bin Laden?'" he asked. I'd never heard the name but went to my office to find out.</p><p>I used to say there were two shocks about Sept. 11 — the first was that it happened, that four planes were hijacked by 19 men wielding box cutters. Two crashed into New York's World Trade Center, toppling the towers. A third hit the Pentagon and a fourth crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers stormed the cockpit; 2,973 men, women and children died that day.</p><p>There was a time when I wouldn't feel obligated to spell out the details. But more than a third of Americans have no living memory of Sept. 11, 2001, and it would not be surprising if 9/11 is news to some — just another crumb of dusty history they didn't learn in school.</p><p>Leading to the second shock of 9/11: that it went away, or at least ebbed. Because for days and weeks and months, it seemed that 9/11 was a permanent condition, a radiating, bottomless shock, sorrow and stupefaction. But ebb it did, slowly receding, like a tide going out. And now 25 years have gone by, and attention must be paid again.</p><p>We put out "Extras" in those days — special editions to update breaking news stories, hawked at newsstands downtown. Our first was headlined "UNSPEAKABLE HORROR" — I remember looking at "Unspeakable" and thinking, "Really? 'Cause we're trying to flippin' speak it." The second was better: "TERROR!" </p><p>I filed an insert to our editorial, then asked the City Desk what I could do to help. Go into the Loop, see what's up. So I went back to the Sears Tower and interviewed disappointed tourists who had planned to visit the Sky Deck. At 111 W. Washington, I watched an employee, ex-Marine Johnny Washington, lower the building's flags to half-mast.</p><p>"This is terrible," he said. </p><p>Back at the newsroom, John Cruickshank, a smart and decent Canadian who was co-editor of the paper, made a little speech. This was the biggest story of our lives, yes, but it is also an enormous human tragedy. We should pray. So we all bowed our head and uttered a little silent prayer, then went back to work. I'm not generally a fan of public displays of piety, but it seemed the right thing to do, and I was grateful.</p><p>I won't attempt to summarize all the bad that came from those attacks. Two needless wars, in Afghanistan and Iraq. Over 7,000 U.S. military deaths — twice the loss of 9/11 — not to forget over 200,000 civilian deaths. I don't recall that being called a genocide. The sweeping, intrusive Patriot Act. George W. Bush tried not to demonize Muslims, but others were not so scrupulous — anti-Islamic hate was a major leg of Donald Trump's winning campaigns, and he barred immigration wholesale from Muslim countries. </p><p>On Sept. 12, 2001, I showed my older boy the front page of the New York Times, its photo of an explosion boiling out of the World Trade Center, and asked him what he thought about the picture, worried how he was processing 9/11's enormity. He said it looked beautiful — he thought it was a flower, a red rose, and I didn't correct him. The horror was very hard to wrap your mind around. It still is.</p>

entries.title: Slowed by injury, White Sox catcher Kyle Teel still has tools for a breakout
entries.summary: <p>Back in June, Kyle Teel’s first home run of the season, was preceded by a talking to in the dugout from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> manager Will Venable.</p><p>The gist: Go easier on yourself. It’ll come.</p><p>Instead, Teel ended up missing another six weeks with an injury, and now he’s likely to finish with fewer than 40-regular season games in his second season in the majors.</p><p>As the Sox guard a slim lead in the American League Central standings, the stakes of every at-bat have risen, and the temptation to press is there for the 24-year-old tapped to be their long-term solution behind the plate.</p><p>Reminded of his conversation with Venable about going easier on himself, Teel conceded, “It’s a great point.”</p><p>“Not trying to do everything at once, not trying to figure everything out at once, is important, while still having the urgency to get to where you want to be,” he told the Sun-Times on Thursday. “My biggest thing is, how can I do a job and put us in the best situation?”</p><p>Teel said his pitch-framing — a huge part of why the Sox regard his defense so highly — is slightly better from last season, going by a small sample. On offense, the two home runs he has popped in five games since returning from his sprained left ankle have lent a glow to his production, but he’s still hitting .195/.271/.377 on the season.</p><p>After the work he did to bulk up and add strength over the winter, that’s not the breakout the Sox had anticipated in the spring.</p><p>“He has bigger movements to get the slack out of his swing,” hitting director Ryan Fuller said. “He has done an amazing job of being stronger, more stable, where those movements just get a little bit more refined and tighter. So it’s not going to be as big of a move to get his swing off.”</p><p>It’s less than 100 plate appearances, but Statcast data shows that Teel is yet <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-hitting-director-ryan-fuller-talks-offensive-improvement-and-the-development-that-remains-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u>another White Sox hitter who has seen a significant jump (3 mph) in bat speed</u></a>. Pulling the ball in the air for power more was his explicit goal last season, and the same data shows he’s catching pitches out in front more than his rookie year, where he hit an impressive .273/.375/.411 but also lifted a mild eight homers in 78 games.</p><p>Perhaps the most encouraging element for Teel is that on the heels of blasting a 96 mph fastball out of the park to right field Tuesday night, his swing feels the same as it always has.</p><p>“The thing is, I’m not trying to pull it in the air, either — I’m just trying to put a good swing on the ball,” he said. “I would love to tell you that I made a huge adjustment, or something feels different than last year. But honestly, swinging the bat, I feel like it all just comes down to getting my at-bats, and that’s something I’m lacking this year, just being hurt. The more at-bats I get, the more settled in I feel.”</p><p>When the Sox fly to St. Louis for this weekend’s series with the Cardinals, they’ll have just 16 games left in their schedule, not much time for settling in.</p><p>“I would just say I focus on my process every single day,” Teel said. “The results aren’t always going to come, but if I can refine my process and accomplish what I want every single at-bat, that’s all I can do. That’s all anyone can do, really.”</p><p>He noted that he needs to downgrade the goal of “accomplish what I want” to more granular goals, such as moving a runner over, swinging at the right pitch or making the opposing pitcher work — not just hitting an 112 mph home run every time.</p><p>But what’s clear even after three separate leg injuries in 2026 is that the Sox are prepared to be patient with Teel long-term — trusting that it’ll come.</p><p>“He’s a guy back there,” Venable said. “We plan on being there as our starting catcher.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>A man was critically injured in a shooting in Humboldt Park Thursday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, whose age wasn’t known, was in the 800 block of North Kedzie Avenue at 5:09 p.m. when he was approached by someone and shot in the face and head, police said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Maine South beats New Trier in Big Ten-bound quarterback showdown
entries.summary: <p>The most anticipated New Trier vs. Maine South matchup in a decade contained all the ingredients for a special night.</p><p>Trevians’ quarterback Jackie Ryder is a Purdue recruit and a late-blooming local star. Jameson Purcell, the Maine South quarterback, has been in the spotlight for three years and is heading to Indiana.</p><p>New Trier opened the season with three wins and arrived in the Super 25 just in time for the showdown with the Hawks.</p><p>Both quarterbacks played well, and the scoring went back and forth until Keaton Vitel’s 98-yard kickoff return touchdown provided the little extra magic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/06/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >No. 13 Maine South</a> needed to pull away with a 35-28 win against the No. 24 Trevians on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/10/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Thursday</a> in Northfield.</p><p>“We were going crazy,” Purcell said. “That is exactly what we needed. [New Trier] scored and then [Vitel] took it to the house. He really just took the air out of them. It was a crucial play. They had momentum, and we took it right from them.”</p><p>Vitel caught an 18-yard touchdown pass from Purcell in the first quarter and was an impact player in the defensive secondary as well.</p><p>Ryder scored on a four-yard run to cut Maine South’s lead to 21-14 midway through the third quarter. But the home crowd barely had a chance to celebrate before Vitel scored.</p><p>“We knew we had to bring some energy,” Vitel said. “They told me to take it up our sideline. All I was thinking was, I’m going to wait and be patient until I see the hole and then I’m going to hit the hole. I saw the hole, and it was just the kicker, and I broke it, and I knew I wasn’t going to go down.”</p><p>New Trier (3-1, 0-1 CSL South) battled back to cut the deficit to 28-21 on a trick-play touchdown pass from Ryder to running back Throy Nightengale Jr. to receiver John Baxter.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2e0000" name="image-2e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4073f87/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/381b1a9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5a6058/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="New Trier's Jackie Ryder (5) looks for a receiver during the game against Maine South. entries.title: Woman fatally shot while driving crashes in Back of the Yards
entries.summary: <p>Police are trying to find the assailant who opened fire, killing a motorist early Friday in the Back of the Yards neighborhood on the South Side. </p><p>Around 12:15 a.m., the 50-year-old woman was driving in the 4500 block of South Wood Street when she was struck by gunfire multiple times, causing her to crash into a parked SUV, Chicago police said. </p><p>The unidentified motorist was taken to Stroger Hospital where she died, police said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Indiana willing to close church while opening doors to Bears
entries.summary: <p>What a waste, shock and pity that Gary's beautiful old City Methodist Church <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/09/05/city-methodist-church-largest-midwest-gary-demolition" >will be demolished</a>. Even in decay, it is far more beautiful than everything sprawled around it.</p><p>One is left to wonder why a state as seemingly affluent as Indiana, which is perfectly comfortable with greasing the primrose path for the McCaskeys into the Hoosier State, couldn’t find its way to preserving an architectural beauty for that debilitated community.</p><p>From here, it looks like more of the haves taking very good care of the haves and ignoring the have-very-littles.</p><p>Shame on Indiana.</p><p><i>Dennis Allen, Wilmette</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-080000" name="module-080000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Change review process for Catholic Church abuse allegations </h3><p>Like the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/26/cleared-of-sex-abuse-claim-pfleger-blasts-unjust-archdiocese-probe" >Rev. Michael Pfleger,</a> I would like to see Chicago's archdiocesan process for reviewing allegations of sexual abuse of minors changed.</p><p>Currently, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.archchicago.org/documents/70111/70567/Clerical+Sexual+Abuse+of+Minors+Policies/2427110f-8095-43ab-872d-1045d74f7e12" target="_blank" >Chicago Archdiocese</a>, following the <a class="Link" href="https://www.usccb.org/resources/2026.07%20Charter-rev%20-%20for%20web.pdf" target="_blank" >U.S. Council of Catholic Bishops</a>, requires<i> </i>that its independent review board include a professional who treats those who've abused minors. But it does not have a parallel requirement to<b> </b>include a member who treats sexually abused minors. </p><p>Including a professional with an understanding of victim/survivor trauma and behavior would help in evaluating the veracity of allegations.</p><p><i>Michele Beaulieux, Milwaukee</i> </p><h3>Judge did South Shore tenants wrong </h3><p>It seems that Cook County Judge Debra Seaton has a strange way of protecting tenants from danger — by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/04/south-shore-immigration-raid-midway-blitz-resident-is-still-homeless" >throwing them on the street</a>. She can call it anything she wants, but the outcome is just the same.</p><p>If there wasn't a raid at the apartment complex at 7500 S. South Shore Drive, those people would still be there.</p><p>Seaton could have offered a timetable and plans to help the former residents, but it would have made her do more work.</p><p>Judges sit so high up on their benches that they detach from humans who scrape by just to live each day. Heartless.</p><p><i>Robert Siegerdt, Mundelein</i></p><h3>Trump’s fleeting name </h3><p>I think people don’t need to worry about Donald Trump’s putting his name everywhere. Yes, it’s disgusting and pathetic. But it’s only a matter of time before his name will be considered anathema. After he’s gone — and he will be gone — his name will be seen as the sign that the country went insane and worshipped the devil. His name will be abolished, and buildings and institutions will get their old names back, or newer more honorable ones. </p><p>It’s only a matter of time.</p><p><i>Lauretta Hart, West Ridge</i></p><h3>Coin con </h3><p>Last week, the U.S. Mint started <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-coin-america-250-gold-817c62abfcec862b8c1ec622e5809ab4" target="_blank" >selling $1 gold-colored</a> finished coins with Donald Trump’s face on them. The coin is made of copper, zinc and nickel. They are selling 25 coins for $61 and 100 coins for $154.50. So it is a $1 coin, but if I buy 25 it averages out to be $2.44 per coin. Seems like another grift from Trump. I will stick with the Susan B. Anthony dollar coin.</p><p><i>Richard Barber, Mount Greenwood</i><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago can fly high, lead the way in protecting migratory birds
entries.summary: <p>"Why can’t I be the MVP of the league?"</p><p>Months after Rose <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s3NVmn51zE0" target="_blank" >asked</a> the question in 2010, he was named the NBA’s youngest MVP at 22. Rose's query, along with the ensuing honor went beyond basketball. It captured the spirit of his hometown. Chicago, along with its residents, has the audacity to declare that its best self has yet to be revealed. It’s a place that consistently defies expectations and changes the narrative surrounding it.</p><p>So when Chicago was singled out as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/03/29/chicago-migratory-birds-city-planning-department-guidelines-priority-editorial" target="_blank" >deadliest city in the country for migratory birds</a> in 2019, I felt that spirit. As an urban ecologist who studies how birds interact with cities, I understand the gravity of the situation. <a class="Link" href="https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/fee.2029?casa_token=4NwZWiQYLO4AAAAA%3AW4oNeI7iIgT9rdz59DQ0gEJu7dKU8g06T25YT3-pDMnNkBf_nk9sS_x1p7bvJ1dbU-cyhht_pxRcAQ" target="_blank" >Research</a> from Cornell’s Lab of Ornithology found that birds in Chicago are heavily exposed to light pollution, which can disorient them. In a single fall morning of 2023, nearly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/10/6/23906778/birds-killed-migration-collision-mccormick-place-lakeside-center" target="_blank" >1,000 birds were killed after they collided</a> into McCormick Place Lakeside Center.</p><p>There are serious concerns we need to address. I've analyzed the numbers and cared for injured birds. I don't mean to downplay the tragedy. But I also see the moment as an opportunity to change the narrative.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-280000" name="module-280000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>The very reason that Cornell study highlighted our city is because we sit along a major migratory flyway, bringing us an astonishing volume of birds passing through. Often, we think of protecting biodiversity as a distant issue. But every spring and fall, we play a direct role in it as our feathered friends fill the sky above our city.</p><p>A study I <a class="Link" href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s44284-025-00388-7" target="_blank" >published</a> earlier this year revealed that metropolitan areas like Chicago play a major role in providing migratory habitat.</p><p>What could it look like if the City of the Big Shoulders embraced its role as a passageway for migratory birds? What could it look like if Chicago took the lead on protecting them?</p><p>We haven’t realized that vision, but I do catch glimpses of what it could look like.</p><p>I see it when I lead bird walks in Humboldt Park and watch people's astonishment when they spot their first chestnut-sided warbler.</p><p>I see it when local birding chats blow up over a rare sighting.</p><p>I see it in the eyes of volunteers monitoring the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/03/23/chicago-piping-plovers-monitors" target="_blank" >piping plovers at Montrose Beach</a> and in the artists painting portraits of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/07/24/black-crowned-night-heron-british-open-world-cup-disability-pride-parade-bars" target="_blank" >black-crowned night herons at Lincoln Park Zoo</a>.</p><p>I saw it when I toured the Chicago Architecture Center’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/12/jeanne-gang-chicago-architecture-center-flyway-openlands-exhibition-birds" target="_blank" >Flyway City Exhibit</a>, which explores how we can design our city around a vision that is hospitable to migratory birds</p><p>Most importantly, I see it in the growing number of Chicagoans who share my resolve to defy expectations and make such a vision a reality.</p><p>In the coming weeks, millions of migratory birds will pass through Chicago while we sleep. Many will stop into our city to rest and refuel. There are various ways we can support them and show our best selves like Rose did 15 years ago. Solutions exist, and we can take the lead on implementing them.</p><p>At a minimum, we can reduce the light pollution we emit at night and treat windows in our homes and workplaces. These simple steps are surprisingly effective and can <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/01/08/bird-collisions-down-mccormick-place-environment" target="_blank" >reduce collisions by 95%</a>. In our green spaces, we can reduce disturbances by keeping our pets away from bird habitats, including native plantings, beaches and forests.</p><p>Systemically, we can advocate for policies like the city's proposed <a class="Link" href="https://birdfriendlychicago.org/ordinance" target="_blank" >bird-friendly building ordinance</a>, which would establish bird-friendly design requirements to prevent bird deaths from building collisions.</p><p>Most importantly, I encourage fellow Chicagoans to look at the birds and take in the beauty of such an ecological wonder. Even a passing moment with a migratory bird offers perspective on our city’s place — and our own place — in this hemispheric marvel. Over and over, I’ve watched such a moment become a steadfast dedication to protecting birds and the ecosystems they depend on.</p><p>Our city can provide the crucial assist for migratory birds if we care to act.</p><p>If a lifetime of Bulls fandom has taught me anything, it's that if Chicago cares about something, the entire world will hear about it.</p><p><i>Miguel "Mikko" Jimenez is an urban ecologist and ornithological adviser to the Windy City Bird Lab. He lives in Avondale.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-780000" name="module-780000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Had falling-out with friend, would like to know details of his death
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My friend "Ben" and I had many ups and downs in our 30-year friendship. Three years ago, we had one of our periodic blowouts and stopped speaking. I found out recently that he passed away a year later, and I was never informed. The obituary I found online does not mention a cause of death.</p><p>I wrote a letter of condolence to his wife, but it was returned, and I found out that she moved away from the house where she and Ben had been living. I would like to know what happened to my friend, as he was only in his early 50s. Although we were not speaking at the time of his death, we had many years of friendship under our belts, and I cared about him. I found a Facebook page for his wife, but this seems an impersonal way of reaching out on such a sober topic. Any suggestions? — <i>CARED FOR HIM IN THE SOUTH</i></p><p><b>DEAR CARED:</b> If you and Ben had mutual friends, a way to find out the information you're looking for, including his widow's address, might be through them. Do it privately. To approach her online asking for the details of his death would be off-putting, insensitive and possibly hurtful in light of the fact that you were estranged at the time of his death.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My 63rd birthday is coming up. I do not like celebrating my birthday and never have. I would prefer that the day be ignored. I know my wife of almost 38 years, our two boys and their significant others are planning something.</p><p>I would prefer they spend the money on themselves or at least donate it to some worthy charity rather than spend it on me. Given that birthdays are important to them, must I just grin and bear it, or should I say something and risk causing ill will? — <i>OLDER IN ISRAEL</i></p><p><b>DEAR OLDER:</b> Surely your wife, who has been with you for nearly four decades, knows your feelings on this subject. Tell her you know something is afoot, and gently mention that you would prefer that the celebration be kept small. Name the charity of your choice, and tell her you hope the birthday budget will be sent there rather than spent on you.</p><p>If your wife ignores your plea and a massive fete does materialize, do your best to endure it with grace and a smile. Remember that these people are celebrating you because they love you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm married, and I've recently started developing a crush on my co-worker. We have worked together for four years. I'm not going to pursue anything, because cheating is against my morals. I just feel bad for having these feelings. What can I do to get my feelings toward my co-worker in check? — <i>CRUSHING IN ILLINOIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR CRUSHING:</b> The guilt you are experiencing is a good thing; it has kept you from making a terrible mistake. If it's any comfort, bear in mind that crushes like this usually lessen in time, even if they make the present somewhat uncomfortable.</p><p><b>TO MY READERS:</b> Happy New Year to my friends of the Jewish faith! During this time of repentance, observant Jews reflect on their lives and make amends, seeking a closer relationship with God. Happy Rosh Hashanah! — <i>LOVE, ABBY</i></p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: As engineer and artist blend styles, Bears' Ben Johnson gets 'goosebumps' about future with Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p>As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> sat in a conference room at Halas Hall one morning during training camp and dreamed out loud about the upcoming season, he rocked with energy in his swivel chair. He leaned forward and talked with no hesitation about going after not only this Super Bowl, but many, and shattering the scoring record.</p><p>And then he brought up <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>, the quarterback he believes can help him do it.</p><p>“I get excited about what this team can become because you’ll see Caleb take the next step,” Johnson told the Sun-Times. “I get goosebumps thinking how far he can go as he masters what we’re asking him to do.”</p><p>That’s where the engineer and artist must come together to create something beautiful. Williams makes stunning plays with his improvisational skills and throws that make you question physics. Johnson’s play designs are all about precision, spacing and timing.</p><p>It’ll take both.</p><p>While Johnson coached Williams like a rookie in their first season together, their second one is about meeting somewhere in the middle. It won’t be exact halfway between their styles, of course, since Johnson still runs this show, but they’re crafting a blend blend as they head into the season opener Sunday at the Panthers.</p><p>As Johnson rose to become one of the NFL’s elite offensive coaches with the Lions, he was fortunate to have a quarterback in Jared Goff who was wired perfectly for him. Everything was clockwork and automatic. He was the physical representation of Johnson’s brain.</p><p>Williams isn’t Goff, but Johnson wants to say two things on that subject:</p><p><b>1. “That doesn’t mean that he can’t share more of those attributes, though.”</b></p><p><b>2. “It’s been fun to coach this guy because... his skillset is different than anybody in the league, much less anybody that I’ve been around.”</b></p><p>Johnson and Williams’ connection will define the Bears’ season. The offense can be a powerhouse if Williams transfers Johnson’s coaching to the pocket by throwing more accurately, recognizing low-risk, high-reward opportunities that are woven into this offense and deciphering defensive coverages deftly.</p><p>All of that would boost his completion percentage from the league-worst 58.1 he posted last season toward Johnson’s benchmark of 70%. The Bears would have their first 4,000-yard passer. Points would pile up. Wins would stack.</p><p>Williams believes it. After a season of Johnson pushing him paid off with progress, he said, “Coaching matters... And then you have to have the person on the other side to receive the coaching.”</p><p>But Johnson’s requirements are exactly that: required. He was dumbfounded when asked at the start of training camp if Williams completing 70% of his passes was still the standard, saying, “It’s always going to be the goal… Always 70%.”</p><p>His conviction runs deep, but so does his creativity, and he saw something irresistible in Williams’ stunning highlights from last season that stirred his imagination. It opened a part of his mind that he’d never explored as a play caller.</p><p>Johnson isolated the 120 plays in which Williams broke the pocket and it turned into a free-for-all. That produced some of his most epic passes, but overall, less than 40% of the time he did that resulted in “good plays for us.”</p><p>That led to two key observations:</p><p><b>1. Johnson showed Williams instances in which it was completely unnecessary to scramble, and a simple sidestep would’ve allowed him to still hit the primary receiver on time.</b></p><p><b>2. Williams can be amazing on the fly, and Johnson needs to make better use of it.</b></p><p>The first point fits with everything Johnson has said since he took the job, but the second is him moving Williams’ direction. He basically built that into the offense this season by creating second layers to plays that are activated once Williams scrambles.</p><p>“We’ll do some things a little bit different,” Johnson said. “He needs to be more accurate, sure, but we need our route runners to come alive to create separation for him also. As a coach, you’re dedicated to teaching the playbook, [but] we don’t want to fully shut that off. We see opportunity there. It’s not that we want to take those 120 plays down; I want to see that 40% go up.</p><p>“It’s a two-way street. That’s what’s been fun about coaching this guy, and it's also a big part of the challenge, too.”</p><p>The Bears believed Williams was a rare talent when they drafted him No. 1 overall and thought the same of Johnson when they hired him last year. But it’s really about what they could become in tandem:</p><p><b>1. Johnson maximizing Williams’ gifts.</b></p><p><b>2. Williams applying Johnson’s expertise.</b></p><p>They want the same things, and they’re essential to each other’s aspirations. Williams saw last season how much better Johnson can make him, and Johnson saw a unique weapon that could make him a more potent play caller. And after months of working behind the scenes, it’s finally time for everyone to see what they’ve built.</p>

entries.title: Evanston Folk Festival puts spotlight on local artists and Chicago’s musical roots and history
entries.summary: <p>Kelly Hogan likes to think of her latest project, Roses for the Roches, as a way of going “door to door” to spread the love for Terre, Maggie and Suzzy Roche, the harmonizing sister trio from New Jersey whom many regard as heroines of ’70s folk.</p><p>“Once you get the Roches fever, you just want to go ringing doorbells, like ding-dong, have you heard this good s---?” said the Wisconsin-based singer who has a long history in the Chicago music scene, including collaborations with Mavis Staples, Andrew Bird and Neko Case. In the Roches tribute project, she’s joined by more local talents, including her Flat Five cohort Nora O’Connor and Sima Cunningham of Chicago indie rock band Finom.</p><p>Having covered a good swath of Chicago, including the trio’s first show at the Old Town School of Folk Music in Lincoln Square in 2017 and the Hideout in West Town last year, Roses for the Roches heads to Evanston Sunday. They’ll perform at the final day of the Evanston Folk Festival, where Hogan hopes attendees will receive her passionate sales pitch that the Roches’ works like “Hammond Song” and “Losing True” significantly shined a light on “the importance of harmony … and had such complexity in the arrangements,” she said, illuminating the dynamic that made many take notice of the Roches, including collaborators like Paul Simon, Robert Fripp and Linda Ronstadt. Though the group essentially ended in 2017 when Maggie died from breast cancer, Roses for the Roches hopes to continue giving the sisters their flowers with a new generation.</p><div entries.title: Attacks against DEI stop America from reaching its full promise
entries.summary: <p>Diversity, equity and inclusion.</p><p>In some circles, those are bad words and uttering them is like spewing three four-letter cuss words in a row.</p><p>There was a time when I viewed those words with hope and promise.</p><p>About a decade ago, during my time with a former employer, I took part in a DEI initiative. For weeks, the entire staff participated in group training sessions around diversity, equity and inclusion.</p><p>Initially, I thought the sessions would largely revolve around people of color sharing their harsh memories of facing marginalization and discrimination, effectively educating their white counterparts about the realities of living in a Eurocentric, white-dominated society with a long history of oppression.</p><p>Indeed, there were conversations where people of color shared heartbreaking stories. Among my examples were being called the N-word, getting stopped by police frequently, seeing my home plummet in value despite spending thousands of dollars for upgrades, meeting in person with sources for the first time who didn’t initially believe I was the reporter with whom they’d spoken, and receiving hate mail from readers who disapproved of stories I’d written about racial inequality.</p><p>But the sessions went much deeper than that.</p><p>I, too, learned a lot from the conversations.</p><p>While life as a Black man in America comes with a heavy burden, I learned that I also live a life of privilege.</p><p>In one of the sessions, we walked through all of the ways we’re different from one another by race, ethnicity, gender, age, income, education, religion, immigration status, sexual orientation, disability status, military experience, and other attributes I don’t always consider.</p><p>As an able-bodied, heterosexual, college-educated, middle-class, Christian, native-born man, I’m spared from the doubts, fears and misperceptions often faced by individuals living with disabilities, members of the LGBTQ+ community, Jews, Muslims, women, immigrants, those without a college degree or individuals who consider themselves working class.</p><p>I learned there are many lines of difference beyond race and ethnicity. And our lack of awareness of the experiences of people who are different from us can lessen our sensitivity to trauma they’ve endured. That ignorance can produce blind spots in how we view their circumstances, conditions and choices of others and, ultimately, manifest as conscious or unconscious bias.</p><p>The rationale for DEI training was that a nonprofit organization of diverse employees serving a diverse Chicago region should be in tune with the nuances and intricacies of difference. DEI training would help us understand the different personal experiences and perspectives of our co-workers. The training would also help us collectively build the skills we needed to better understand the inequitable conditions that our organization was committed to address. In short, DEI would not only help us work better together, but it would also improve the quality and effectiveness of our mission-driven work.</p><p>It all made sense to me.</p><p>But, in the years since, while the promise for what America can accomplish with DEI remains, my hope that we will ever take the necessary steps to realize that promise is beginning to fade.</p><p>The lofty goals of DEI have been hijacked — they’ve been overpoliticized and overracialized.</p><p>There’s nothing inherently political about creating a space for us to acknowledge the many ways we’re different from one another. There’s nothing Democratic or Republican about examining how those differences affect our perceptions of each other. And there’s nothing liberal or conservative about recognizing the strengths we obtain through a diverse workforce to limit our collective blind spots.</p><p>And DEI is not about racial quotas or hiring unqualified people. It isn’t anti-white or anti-male. The training doesn’t choose sides. There are ways in which we’ve all felt marginalized. For sure, there are people who’ve felt it through multiple lanes of identity, but we’ve all felt diminished or overlooked at some point in our lives in some way or another. Tapping into those feelings and recognizing that we’ve all experienced pain due to the ignorance and bias of others could serve as a way we can achieve common ground in spite of our differences.</p><p>However, the past few years have shown that — at least, for now — we’re still too comfortable with our hate and indifference. We’re still too susceptible to messages that those who are different from us are our enemies. But the reality, I believe, is that our resistance to finding our commonality is our true enemy. Like the nonprofit organization that introduced me to DEI, our nation can’t work well together nor pursue its mission if its residents remain so focused on and divided by our differences.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/author/alden-loury" target="_blank" ><i>Alden Loury</i></a><i> is data projects editor for WBEZ and writes a column for the Sun-Times.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-180000" name="module-180000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: A reporter followed Chicago first responders to New York after 9/11. He saw devastation — and heroism
entries.summary: <p>Everybody has a 9/11 story.</p><p>Mine begins three days earlier, in an apple orchard outside Saratoga Springs, N.Y.</p><p>One of my best friends from college was getting married. He lived in New York City and some of his buddies at the wedding worked at the World Trade Center.</p> <p>It was a glorious weekend of bluegrass music and Calvados apple brandy. We flew home Sept. 10, 2001.</p><p>Then the world stopped turning.</p><p>On the morning of Sept. 11, I was driving down the Eisenhower Expressway, listening to the radio as I headed downtown to work.</p><p>Network news reporters broke into the show from New York.</p><p>The first plane had hit.</p><p>Then the second.</p><p>Stunned, I called my wife to tell her to turn on the TV as the Sears Tower loomed closer and closer in my windshield.</p><p>Was Chicago next?</p><p>Later, I called home to check on my family. I also reached my friend in New York.</p><p>To my relief, his Wall Street buddies were safe.</p><p>On Sept. 13, O’Hare Airport reopened and a flight was heading to White Plains, just outside New York City.</p><p>My editors booked tickets for me, fellow reporter Bryan Smith and photographer Robert A. Davis. We raced through the airport and made the flight.</p><p>The assignment seemed simple enough: Find the Chicago cops and firefighters who had dropped everything and rushed to New York to help — and follow them.</p><p>But nothing about those days was simple.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b20000" name="image-b20000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3a6dc23/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+188/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8e%2F4d%2F95eca87c434cb708cde7d7edc5a7%2Fterror-attacks.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4732c33/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+188/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8e%2F4d%2F95eca87c434cb708cde7d7edc5a7%2Fterror-attacks.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/02fec8a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+188/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8e%2F4d%2F95eca87c434cb708cde7d7edc5a7%2Fterror-attacks.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Firefighters make their way through the rubble after two airliners crashed into the World Trade Center in New York bringing down the landmark buildings Tuesday, Sept. 10, 2001. entries.title: Construction sites will be required to be more welcoming to women under a new Illinois law
entries.summary: <p>Zahrah Hill, a foreman and plumber from the West Side, returned to her construction job three months after giving birth to her son and, as a breastfeeding mother, she didn’t have a space to safely express milk.</p><p>In a matter of months, female construction workers like Hill and others who lactate or menstruate won’t have that same problem under a state law Gov. JB Pritzker signed last month.</p><p>It’s the culmination of a legislative push in Springfield to make the state’s predominantly male construction industry embrace a new level of diversity that hasn’t existed since Chicago was credited as the place that invented skyscrapers.</p><p>Hill says that recognition is long overdue. She remembers how, as a new mom, she had to resort to desperate measures after going all day without pumping while on her job site.</p><p>“I was literally expressing milk into an old coffee cup and dumping it out the window on the way home,” she said. “Just mashing down on my breasts and dumping it out just to relieve some of the pressure.”</p><p>She said she eventually reached out to her superintendent, and started bringing her breast-pumping supplies and a mini-fridge to work.</p><p>“I came in every morning, and I plugged my refrigerator in so that it got nice and cold,” she said. “And, on my break, he would clear out of his office, and I would sit in his office and express milk.”</p><p>She said while she made it work, “I was, like, you know what, something's got to give.”</p><p>According to a report from the Institute for Women’s Policy Research, women make up just over 4% of the construction labor workforce nationally. In Illinois, the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis reported, nearly 253,000 construction industry jobs last month.</p><p>It’s evident that women make up a meaningful presence on construction worksites — and that presence is growing. In 2024, the number of women in construction hit a record high nationally, up by nearly 80% from 2015.</p><p>And it’s that part of the construction workforce that figures to benefit most from the new law, which advocates say could bring more women into the trades.</p><p>Starting in January, construction worksites with female workers and more than 10 employees will be required to provide accommodations for menstruation and lactation.</p><p>Illinois is the second state to adopt these requirements, which take effect in January. Washington did so in 2024.</p><p>“Construction sites historically haven't necessarily been the most welcoming environments for many women,” said state Sen. Graciela Guzman, D-Chicago, who championed the legislation. “Bathrooms, in themselves, have been a potential tool for harassment or unequal treatment.”</p><p>Under the new law, employers will have to provide a designated women’s restroom with an internal lock, and women who are breastfeeding will be able to request a sanitary place to express milk.</p><p>Also, construction employers will have to provide a minimum of 10 menstrual products like tampons or pads, a refrigerator to store breast milk and running water to wash hands or breast-pumping equipment.</p><p>Chicago Women in Trades, an organization that works to eliminate barriers for women in the trade industry, brought the bill to Guzman. Beth Berendsen, the group's policy director, said that, in addition to the accommodations, those who menstruate or lactate also will get adequate time to use the bathroom.</p><p>“It is a big challenge with women in construction often wearing many layers of clothing, especially in the winter time or under certain circumstances, to have to remove the layers of clothing to do what they need to do in the restroom,” she said.</p><p>Berendsen said some women reported not having easy access to a restroom while the men’s was easily reachable. They also say they face bullying for the time they spend in the bathroom.</p><p>“It’s different than what a lot of men do, and so they end up taking longer and can sometimes be punished for that,” she said.</p><p>Critics of the legislation cited concerns about the measures employers on job sites will have to provide and about how to provide accommodations on mobile worksites such as highways.</p><p>The National Federation of Business and Associated Builders and Contractors of Illinois opposed the legislation. Neither organization responded to requests for comment.</p><p>The law allows for exceptions. For instance, if there are temporary workers who menstruate or lactate and will be on site for only two days, employers don’t have to provide the otherwise-required accommodations. Workers who are lactating must request the accommodations they need, and employers can refuse under concerns of “undue hardship" — that is, if providing the accommodations would pose a safety risk or be disruptive or prohibitively expensive.</p><p>Berendsen said the costs should be minimal because there are so few women on worksites.</p><p>“One thing that we do hear from employers is about workforce shortages, and that really means we cannot be turning down half of the population when we need to hire for these jobs and these positions,” she said. “What we do know is that diverse and inclusive work sites produce better outcomes.”</p><p>Hill, 34, said she hopes the new requirements bring more women into the workforce.</p><p>“Guys, in general, just don't think about things like these,” she said. “There are women on your job sites that are pregnant, will become pregnant and are mothers. We are not asking to show up to work for half the time and get the full pay. We're just asking for small accommodations to make it better for us.”</p>

entries.title: A year of silence follows ICE killing of Silverio Villegas González, despite resounding calls for justice
entries.summary: <p>The first police report on Silverio Villegas González’s death is seven sentences long.</p><p>It doesn’t name the immigration agent who shot him.</p><p>It doesn’t identify any witnesses, or the FBI personnel who showed up to investigate.</p><p>And it says nothing about the gun that was used.</p><p>Little about the case has been revealed since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/12/ice-officer-fatally-shoots-man-during-traffic-stop-in-chicago-suburb-authorities-say" target="_blank" >Villegas González was fatally shot</a> by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on Sept. 12, 2025 — four days after the Trump administration <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/morning-edition/2025/09/09/trump-midway-blitz-ice-justice-department-chicago-bears-soybean" target="_blank" >launched Operation Midway Blitz</a>, the deportation campaign that rocked the Chicago area last fall.</p><p>Villegas González had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/13/man-fatally-shot-by-ice-officer-in-franklin-park-is-identified" target="_blank" >dropped his kids off at school</a> and was headed to work when two ICE agents tried to stop his car in Franklin Park and one of them opened fire. Villegas González had immigrated from Mexico and was targeted because he didn't have legal status in the U.S.</p><p>Over the past year, his family and community has been left to grapple with painful, unanswered questions as interest in the case has waned.</p><p>The FBI won’t discuss its investigation, and the Department of Homeland Security has said that federal prosecutors declined to charge the agent who fired the deadly shots. Now, the Illinois State Police has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/05/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-trump-silverio-villegas-gonzalez" target="_blank" >opened an investigation</a>.</p><p>But Jonathan Manes, an attorney with the MacArthur Justice Center who represents Villegas González’s family, says the lack of information has been troubling<b>.</b></p><p>“It’s shocking that a year after the shooting, the federal government has refused to release any information about ICE officers that took a man’s life on our streets,” Manes says. “They haven’t even provided the name of the officer who shot Silverio and killed him.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure There may have been other drivers or witnesses who could have provided firsthand accounts of the shooting, Manes says, but there’s no record of any statements.</p><p>Those witnesses could have helped establish where the ICE agent was standing when he fired. Villegas González was shot in the neck, suggesting the agent was alongside Villegas González’s vehicle when he fired — rather than directly in its path, Manes says.</p><p>It’s also unclear what happened to the ICE agent’s gun after the shooting.</p><p>Records from Franklin Park indicate the weapon was left at the scene with local cops, Manes says. But the records don’t say who ultimately took possession of the gun, or where it was sent.</p><p>“The weapon is an extremely important piece of evidence in any shooting," Manes says. "And the fact that there’s no documentation at all about who had it, who it was given to, is pretty striking."</p><p>Franklin Park quickly handed over the shooting investigation to the FBI. But Manes says his team still doesn’t know what federal investigators found.</p><p>Franklin Park officials didn't respond to requests for comment. </p><p>Mayor Barrett Pedersen previously said the village never probed the shooting because police were told by DHS that the FBI would investigate.</p><p>“I continue to call on the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI to provide complete transparency regarding the results of their investigation into the death of Silverio Villegas González,” Pedersen wrote in May. “His family, and our community demand to know the results of their investigation.”</p><p>Homeland Security officials continue to say that Villegas González tried to flee a traffic stop and injured an officer by dragging him “a significant distance.” They complained of “disgusting” smears and misleading reporting.</p><p>But their credibility has been significantly damaged by other false or unproven claims tied to Midway Blitz. That’s in addition to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >a series of failed prosecutions</a> tied to the campaign.</p><p>Villegas González’s family is calling for justice and want his name cleared.</p><p>“The administration has tried to justify his death by smearing his good name with lies and false narratives,” according to his brother, José Villegas González, and sister-in-law, Ana Villegas. </p><p>“A year has not erased or diminished the ache we feel in his absence.”</p><h3><b>A year without answers</b></h3><p>Once on scene, Franklin Park police scrambled to figure out who had jurisdiction over the shooting investigation, according to body camera footage. The commission concluded that “federal agents shot and killed Villegas González without apparent justification.”</p><p>In the request to ISP, Franklin Park police indicated the department didn’t have any evidence logs, use-of-force reports or photos from the scene.</p><p>The ISP investigation is still open, according to an agency spokesperson. entries.title: Mayor Daley's argument that he shuttered Meigs Field out of post-9/11 security concerns never seemed credible
entries.summary: <p>As concert-goers stream onto Northerly Island this weekend to catch a show by the South Side’s own Chief Keef at an outdoor theater, they may not realize there used to be a different type of buzz there: Of planes taking off and landing at a little airport called Meigs Field.</p><p>But Chicagoans of a certain age may recall its controversy: The general aviation airfield, with a single runway and a stubby control tower, occupied the artificial island starting in the late 1940s, ultimately catering to aviation enthusiasts, along with business and government types gaining easy access — via jets, prop planes and choppers — to the Loop.</p><p>At least until 2003.</p><p>That’s when Chicago’s then-mayor, Richard M. Daley, abruptly closed the airfield by quietly ordering in heavy machinery to carve giant X marks in the 3,900-foot-long runway, rendering the site inoperable. There was no advance notice, except perhaps a backdoor tip off to select powerbrokers.</p><p>Daley explained that it was a post-9/11 security measure, with the airfield in the midst of all those high-rises, and he insisted he couldn’t jeopardize Chicago’s safety and security — though the explanation was never quite credible.</p><p>He’d wanted for years — well before 9/11 — to convert the plot into open green space, only to face resistance from flying advocates, businesspeople and state officials including then-Gov. entries.title: Restoring small-town charm in Roanoke, Indiana
entries.summary: <p><i>Regenerative tourism harnesses the power of sustainable travel to transform places and communities for the better. In this series, we look at Midwestern towns and small cities that have leaned into tourism to help lift local economies and create destinations that travelers want to visit.</i></p><p>Tiny Roanoke, about 10 miles south of Fort Wayne, makes a disarming first impression. Flower baskets and American flags hang from street lamps in front of restored buildings along a handsome 19th-century main street. Clothing boutiques and galleries fill refurbished storefronts interspersed with cafes and restaurants. Occasionally, elementary school students practice “plein air” painting downtown.</p><p>“I can drive my golf cart anywhere I want,” says Lee Ann Smith, the treasurer of the Roanoke Fall Festival and a 10-year town resident who moved to Roanoke when she fell “madly in love with the small-town feel.”</p><p>It wasn’t always so Mayberry. On the hunting grounds of Miami Indians, Roanoke flourished with the construction of the 468-mile Wabash & Erie Canal, which connected Toledo, Ohio to Evansville in the mid-1800s. A lock on the canal at Roanoke brought trade and traffic to town. It was later supplanted by the railroad. Eventually, Roanoke began to decline after World War II, losing its Main Street appeal to suburbs and shopping malls. By the 1980s, its retail core was largely abandoned.</p><h3>A renaissance in rural Indiana </h3><p>In 1990, Pete Eshelman, a former Yankees pitcher then working in Fort Wayne, chose tiny Roanoke to open a sports and entertainment insurance company called American Specialty. He began buying old buildings downtown and eventually opened the fine-dining restaurant <a class="Link" href="https://josephdecuis.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Joseph Decuis</u></a> (191 N. Main St.) specializing in wagyu beef that he and his family raised on their farm outside of town.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Main St., makes an excellent wagyu burger. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“‘Our corporate life and the renaissance of Roanoke are inextricably intertwined,” wrote Eshelman in a book he co-authored, “Roanoke, The Renaissance of a Hoosier Village.”</p><p>Though local favorites like the <a class="Link" href="https://roanokevillageinn.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Roanoke Village Inn</u></a> (190 N. Main St.), which dates to 1946, predated Joseph Decuis, the Eshelmans seeded the Roanoke’s incarnation as a foodie stronghold in rural Indiana, eventually opening the more casual Joseph Decuis Emporium (151 N. Main St.). “They have excellent gumbo and wagyu burgers, which are not things you can usually get in small town restaurants,” says John Nelson, a financial advisor and the board president of the Roanoke Beautification Foundation.</p><p>Other openings followed, adding diversity. <a class="Link" href="https://thecopperstillroanoke.com/" target="_blank" ><u>The Copper Still</u></a> (165 S. Main St.) specializes in bourbon, whiskey and cocktails served alongside a robust menu of salads, sandwiches and entrees. Play dates meet up at the <a class="Link" href="https://theparkergracetearoom.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Parker Grace Tea Room</u></a> (138 W. First St.) tucked in a Victorian home for its vintage décor, light bites and desserts.</p><p>Between bites, Roanoke visitors can stop into its history museum or browse its many boutiques – among them <a class="Link" href="https://savinggracevintage.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Saving Grace Vintage</u></a> (212 N. Main St.) for furnishings, <a class="Link" href="https://ashivelyandco.com/" target="_blank" ><u>A. Shively & Co.</u></a> (138 W. First St.) for housewares with an organic bent and <a class="Link" href="https://www.roanokeoutdoordistrict.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Outdoor District</u></a> (159 N. Main St.) for men’s and women’s gear – that have helped make Roanoke a popular destination.</p><p>Nelson’s Roanoke Beautification Foundation designed Zent Commons on Main, an urban plaza with a fire pit inspired by ski resorts as a place to gather. He calls the town “borderline Norman Rockwell” and credits the all-hands approach of supportive residents. “If someone has an idea and checks the boxes and gets permission from the right entities, you can pretty much do any kind of event here you want,” he says.</p><p><b>Other things to do:</b><br>Through crash and recovery, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.roanokefallfestival.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Roanoke Fall Festival</u></a> has celebrated all things autumn. Now in its 72nd year, the weekend event, Sept. 10-12, features parades, a tractor pull, craft vendors, pie and ice cream eating contests, a baked goods competition, pig races and a rodeo as well as food and music.</p><p>Outside of town, parks are big attractions in surrounding Huntington County, including the recently expanded <a class="Link" href="https://www.in.gov/dnr/state-parks/parks-lakes/salamonie-lake/" target="_blank" ><u>Salamonie Lake State Park</u></a> protecting the namesake reservoir and surroundings popular with hikers and fishermen. <a class="Link" href="https://www.rusticriveroutfitters.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Rustic Rivers Outfitters</u></a> in the village of Mt. Etna offers canoe and kayak trips on the Salamonie and Wabash Rivers (6062 W. 600 S., Huntington). Thrill-seekers can ride eight zip lines and traverse four aerial bridges at <a class="Link" href="http://www.discovertimberlake.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Camp Timber Lake</u></a> about five miles south of Roanoke (1740 E. 675 N., Huntington). Don’t miss the <a class="Link" href="https://www.huntington.in.us/egov/apps/locations/facilities.egov?view=detail&id=50" target="_blank" ><u>Sunken Gardens</u></a> in Huntington created of an abandoned quarry (1125 W. Park Dr., Huntington).</p><p>Near Camp Timber Lake, <a class="Link" href="https://twoees.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Two-EE’s Winery</u></a> offers glasses, flights, tastings, slushies and bottles of its estate-grown wines (6808 N. US Highway 24, Huntington). A dog-friendly outdoor patio and lawn host concerts, outdoor movies and trivia nights.</p><p><b>Where to stay:</b><br>Live like a townie in a downtown <a class="Link" href="https://www.airbnb.com/rooms/54115722?search_mode=regular_search&adults=1&check_in=2026-08-22&check_out=2026-08-27&children=0&infants=0&pets=0&source_impression_id=p3_1787179455_P3BYDwhIuLInJC0y&previous_page_section_name=1000&federated_search_id=6f71a2be-8de2-4e7c-96c8-3ab4a890f686" target="_blank" ><u>home on Airbnb</u></a>. Just north of Roanoke, the <a class="Link" href="https://josephdecuis.com/farmstead" target="_blank" ><u>Joseph Decuis Farmstead Inn</u></a> (6756 E. 900 S., Columbia City) offers six bedrooms in restored 1884 farm buildings including a farmhouse, carriage house and barn.</p>
